1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
5	This process can be triggered by vanishingly small synthetic fractions~\cite{dohmatob2025strong}: lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the biases of its predecessors.
6	As machine-generated text grows prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing risk to production pipelines, and by the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
7	
8	This threat motivates a fundamental question: \emph{what does the detectability landscape of model collapse look like?}
9	At what contamination level does statistical detection become possible, how does this boundary depend on observation length, and what structure does the landscape exhibit?
10	These questions are nontrivial because iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points), where detection power drops sharply~\cite{boettiger2012limits}. Moreover, model collapse is a first-order transition~\cite{truong2026phase}, structurally ruling out the critical-slowing-down early-warning signals that ecologists rely on~\cite{scheffer2009early} (\S\ref{sec:related_work}).
11	
12	We map this landscape on Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across 13 contamination levels with multi-seed replication (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}), and find structured terrain rather than smooth degradation: detection is absent through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jumps from 0/8 to 6/8 significant pairs within a 2-percentage-point interval, before a non-monotonic dip and eventual reliable detection above a power-law boundary $\alpha_c(T)$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:alpha-c-theory}).
13	Cross-architecture evaluation at $\alpha{=}1.0$ across five families (345M--6.9B) supports forward detection in 11/15 conditions, with four non-confirming cases isolating distinct failure modes (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
14	A second finding is equally consequential: five statistical methods applied to identical data yield null-control false-positive rates from 3\% to 92\%, demonstrating that the landscape one observes depends critically on the method used to probe it.
15	Our canary claim\footnote{Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causation~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; bivariate tests cannot exclude confounders.} is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}).
16	
17	Our contributions are:
18	\begin{enumerate}
19	    \item \textbf{We characterize the detectability landscape} of iterative model collapse (\S\ref{sec:regime}--\ref{sec:intervention}).
20	    On Pythia-410M (cross-architecture at $\alpha{=}1.0$), PermG identifies a power-law detection boundary $\alpha_c(T)$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:alpha-c-theory}; LOO-CV: MAE${=}0.037$, 15/15 within CI): any nonzero contamination produces signal, but sub-linear growth makes detection a function of $T$.
21	    Canary-triggered cessation substantially reduces peak perplexity in a proof-of-concept intervention ($N{=}2$, $\alpha{=}1.0$).
22	
23	    \item \textbf{We establish a formal design rationale for canary metric selection} (\S\ref{sec:cascade}).
24	    Under mode amplification, entropy responds before diversity by ${\geq}1$ generation (Design Principles~\ref{thm:entropy_leads}--\ref{prop:div_lag}), confirmed in 14/15 experiments ($\alpha \geq 0.30$; GPT-2-medium s43 bidirectional).
25	
26	    \item \textbf{We document method sensitivity as a primary finding} (\S\ref{sec:mmct}--\ref{sec:dose_response}).
27	    Five methods yield null-control FPR from 3\% to 92\%; the same Granger test shifts from 0/8 to 6/8 within 2 percentage points, demonstrating that the landscape one observes depends on the method used to probe it.
28	\end{enumerate}
29

33	\caption{Detection phase diagram (Pythia-410M, fp32, PermG direction-checked). Each cell shows the number of FDR-significant canary$\to$diversity pairs (of~8) at a given contamination strength~$\alpha$ and observation window~$T$. \subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:mmct}
We compare five lead-lag detection methods in a multi-method comparison~\cite{simonsohn2020specification} (algorithm in Appendix~\ref{app:mmct}), calibrated against null-control ($\alpha{=}0.0$) data where any detection is a false positive.
PermG's empirical FPR of 11.1\% (CI $[1.2\%, 30.4\%]$; 6 null seeds) exceeds the nominal 5\% threshold; all detection claims are therefore conditioned on MMCT consensus ($K{\geq}3$), which maintains 0\% FPR.
The five methods are: naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation (DiffXCorr), threshold onset, permutation Granger causality (PermG), and Toda--Yamamoto~\cite{toda1995statistical}.
Detection results use equal-weight majority voting ($K{\geq}3$ of 5 methods, each contributing one vote per pair) with forward-direction filtering; FPR-inverse weighting is used only in exploratory method ranking (Appendix~\ref{app:weight_robustness}).
Each method encodes different assumptions, and these differences produce dramatically different FPR profiles.
Pooled null-control FPR across six seeds (6-pair basis, 36 pairs): DiffXCorr 2.8\%, PermG 11.1\%, Threshold 27.8\%, Toda--Yamamoto 38.9\%, NaiveXCorr 91.7\% (Appendix~\ref{app:fpr_independence}).
We classify a method as \emph{directional} if its test structure inherently separates forward from reverse precedence (PermG tests each direction independently; threshold onset compares crossing order), rather than inferring direction post-hoc from peak lag sign (NaiveXCorr, DiffXCorr).
Although DiffXCorr achieves the lowest raw FPR (1/36, 2.8\%), it is bidirectional and cannot distinguish forward from reverse precedence, making it unsuitable as a standalone collapse detector.
PermG (4/36, 11.1\%; cluster-adjusted 95\% CI $[1.2\%, 30.4\%]$) is the lowest-FPR directional method with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ across all four weighting schemes (Shapley analysis: Appendix~\ref{app:shapley}).
Practitioner-facing alternatives (PPL-slope, variance thresholds) yield 67--100\% FPR under natural training drift (Appendix~\ref{app:naive_baselines}).
That method choice alone can shift conclusions from universal significance to complete null on identical data motivates reporting method sensitivity as a primary result rather than relegating it to a robustness check.

\paragraph{Permutation Granger causality.}
PermG tests whether past values of canary metric $X$ improve prediction of downstream metric $Y$ beyond $Y$'s own history~\cite{shojaie2022granger}.
We use classical rather than neural Granger methods~\citep{tank2021neural} because $T{\leq}25$ provides insufficient observations for neural network parameter estimation, and apply 5{,}000 permutations~\citep{phipson2010permutation} on first-differenced series with Benjamini--Hochberg FDR correction at $q{=}0.05$ across 8 canary$\to$downstream pairs (2 canaries $\times$ 4 downstream metrics, sharing canary terms and thus positively dependent).

The permutation null controls Type~I error exactly by construction; BH-FDR remains valid under positive regression dependence on a subset (PRDS)~\cite{benjamini2001control} (assumption discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:fpr_independence}).

\subsection{Cross-Architecture Validation}
\label{sec:generalization}

To test whether the phase-diagram structure is Pythia-specific, we evaluate PermG across 15 model-seed combinations spanning five families, scales 345M--6.9B, and two domains (Table~\ref{tab:generalization}).
Forward detection reaches ${\geq}6/8$ in 11/15 conditions, confirming that PermG generalizes to architectures satisfying the monotonic entropy decline assumption (Design Principle~\ref{thm:entropy_leads}).
Domain matters: C4 yields the strongest detection (Pythia-1.4B: 2/8 WikiText $\to$ 8/8 C4), suggesting that domain-specific mode structure affects detectability.
The four non-confirming conditions each isolate a distinct failure mode: precision sensitivity (GPT-2 bf16: 0/8 vs fp32: 6/8), bidirectional confounding (GPT-2 s43), seed dependence (Pythia-1.4B: s42 2/8, s43 6/8), and entropy decoupling (SmolLM3-3B: 3/8, whose non-monotonic entropy violates Design Principle~\ref{thm:entropy_leads}).

\label{sec:intervention}

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Lead-lag analysis in iterative training collapse is far more fragile than the current literature assumes.
Method choice alone inflates spurious-signal rates to at least 62.5\%, first-differencing exposes canary$\to$perplexity associations as entirely spurious, and regime dependence causes the same Granger test to shift from 24/24 to 0/8 significant pairs across contamination levels.
These design considerations establish that single-method, single-regime analyses (the current default) cannot reliably distinguish genuine temporal precedence from statistical artifacts.

Our systematic five-method comparison through the Multi-Method Consensus Test (MMCT) identifies permutation Granger causality as the recommended detection method: it combines the lowest null-control FPR among directionally-specific methods (11.1\%, 4/36 across 6 seeds; DiffXCorr achieves 2.8\% but lacks directional separation) with high sensitivity, exhibiting a steep dose-response onset from 0/8 (blind spot, $\alpha{\leq}0.45$) to 6/8 ($\alpha{=}0.50$; sigmoid $k{=}15.7$, ${\approx}3{\times}$ steeper than smooth-signal predictions) with reliable detection at $\alpha{\geq}0.75$.
The other four methods each fail in characteristic ways: naive cross-correlation inflates FPR to 75\%, differenced cross-correlation cannot separate forward from reverse precedence, threshold onset is power-limited at $T{=}10$ under $3\sigma$ calibration, and Toda--Yamamoto Granger provides supplementary detection at reduced power (directional assignment under verification).

Applying permutation Granger, token entropy exhibits robust one-generation-ahead precedence over diversity collapse at $\alpha{=}1.0$ on WikiText-103 (24/24 forward, 0/24 reverse across 4~seeds, replicated on GPT-2-medium and OPT-1.3B), with cross-architecture validation confirming forward detection (${\geq}6/8$) in 11 of 15 model-seed combinations spanning five families (345M--6.9B); non-confirming conditions span precision sensitivity (GPT-2 bf16), seed dependence (Pythia-1.4B), entropy decoupling (SmolLM3), and bidirectional confounding (GPT-2 s43).
Directional asymmetry is domain-dependent: consistent unidirectionality holds on WikiText across all regimes, while C4 exhibits near-symmetric bidirectional coupling at $\alpha{=}0.50$ (PermG reverse 7/8), though forward detection remains robust in both domains.
This finding is deliberately scoped to lexical diversity, not model collapse broadly, since the perplexity channel proved entirely spurious under differencing.

The design considerations we expose arise from generic properties of short, non-stationary time series.
Cross-architecture (five families, 345M--6.9B), cross-scale ($3.4\times$ within Pythia), and cross-domain (C4) validation confirms that both the design considerations and the method recommendation are not specific to a single experimental configuration; evaluation on models at ${>}$7B parameters remains an open direction.
Limitations are detailed in \S\ref{sec:limitations}; future directions are discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	When language models train iteratively on their own output, the training distribution progressively loses its tail modes, a phenomenon termed model collapse~\cite{shumailov2024curse,alemohammad2024mad}.
5	This process can be triggered by vanishingly small synthetic fractions~\cite{dohmatob2025strong}: lexical diversity narrows, calibration deteriorates, and each generation inherits the biases of its predecessors.
6	As machine-generated text grows prevalent on the web, such feedback loops pose a growing risk to production pipelines, and by the time standard quality metrics register degradation, the distribution may have already shifted irreversibly.
7	
8	This threat motivates a fundamental question: \emph{what does the detectability landscape of model collapse look like?}
9	At what contamination level does statistical detection become possible, how does this boundary depend on observation length, and what structure does the landscape exhibit?
10	These questions are nontrivial because iterative training produces short, noisy time series (often fewer than 15 points), where detection power drops sharply~\cite{boettiger2012limits}. Moreover, model collapse is a first-order transition~\cite{truong2026phase}, structurally ruling out the critical-slowing-down early-warning signals that ecologists rely on~\cite{scheffer2009early} (\S\ref{sec:related_work}).
11	
12	We map this landscape on Pythia-410M~\cite{biderman2023pythia} across 13 contamination levels with multi-seed replication (Figure~\ref{fig:regime_map}), and find structured terrain rather than smooth degradation: detection is absent through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jumps from 0/8 to 6/8 significant pairs within a 2-percentage-point interval, before a non-monotonic dip and eventual reliable detection above a power-law boundary $\alpha_c(T)$ (Eq.~\ref{eq:alpha-c-theory}).
13	Exploratory cross-architecture evaluation at the single extreme condition $\alpha{=}1.0$ across five families (345M--6.9B) supports forward detection in 11/15 conditions, with four non-confirming cases isolating distinct failure modes (\S\ref{sec:generalization}).
14	A second finding is equally consequential: five statistical methods applied to identical data yield null-control false-positive rates from 3\% to 92\%, demonstrating that the landscape one observes depends critically on the method used to probe it.
15	Our canary claim\footnote{Granger precedence establishes temporal predictive improvement, not true causation~\cite{shojaie2022granger}; bivariate tests cannot exclude confounders.} is scoped to diversity metrics (distinct-$n$~\cite{li2016diversity}).
16	
17	Our contributions are:
18	\begin{enumerate}
19	    \item \textbf{We map the detectability landscape} of iterative model collapse (\S\ref{sec:regime}--\ref{sec:dose_response}).
20	    Detection is absent through $\alpha{=}0.45$, then jumps from 0/8 to 6/8 within 2 percentage points; a detection boundary consistent with power-law scaling $\alpha_c(T) \propto T^{-\gamma}$ ($\gamma \in [0.64, 2.08]$; Eq.~\ref{eq:alpha-c-theory}) organizes three confirmed regimes (blind, onset, detection) plus one unexplained non-monotonic anomaly.
21	
22	    \item \textbf{We document method sensitivity as a primary finding} (\S\ref{sec:mmct}).

25	    \item \textbf{We formalize cascade ordering for canary metric selection} (\S\ref{sec:cascade}).

\subsection{Method Sensitivity Analysis}
\label{sec:mmct}
We compare five lead-lag detection methods in a multi-method comparison~\cite{simonsohn2020specification} (algorithm in Appendix~\ref{app:mmct}), calibrated against null-control ($\alpha{=}0.0$) data where any detection is a false positive.
PermG's empirical FPR of 11.1\% (CI $[1.2\%, 30.4\%]$; 6 null seeds) exceeds the nominal 5\% threshold; $K{\geq}3$ consensus yields 16.7\% FPR (6/36), driven primarily by high-FPR methods (PermG contributes to only 2/6 consensus false positives; Appendix~\ref{app:fpr_independence}).
The five methods are: naive cross-correlation, differenced cross-correlation (DiffXCorr), threshold onset, permutation Granger causality (PermG), and Toda--Yamamoto~\cite{toda1995statistical}.
Detection results use equal-weight majority voting ($K{\geq}3$ of 5 methods, each contributing one vote per pair) with forward-direction filtering; FPR-inverse weighting is used only in exploratory method ranking (Appendix~\ref{app:weight_robustness}).
Each method encodes different assumptions, and these differences produce dramatically different FPR profiles.
Pooled null-control FPR across six seeds (6-pair basis, 36 pairs): DiffXCorr 2.8\%, PermG 11.1\%, Threshold 27.8\%, Toda--Yamamoto 38.9\%, NaiveXCorr 91.7\% (Appendix~\ref{app:fpr_independence}).
We classify a method as \emph{directional} if its test structure inherently separates forward from reverse precedence (PermG tests each direction independently; threshold onset compares crossing order), rather than inferring direction post-hoc from peak lag sign (NaiveXCorr, DiffXCorr).
Although DiffXCorr achieves the lowest raw FPR (1/36, 2.8\%), it is bidirectional and cannot distinguish forward from reverse precedence, making it unsuitable as a standalone collapse detector.
PermG (4/36, 11.1\%; cluster-adjusted 95\% CI $[1.2\%, 30.4\%]$) is the lowest-FPR directional method with consistent detection at $\alpha \geq 0.50$ across all four weighting schemes (Shapley analysis: Appendix~\ref{app:shapley}).
Practitioner-facing alternatives (PPL-slope, variance thresholds) yield 67--100\% FPR under natural training drift (Appendix~\ref{app:naive_baselines}).
That method choice alone can shift conclusions from universal significance to complete null on identical data motivates reporting method sensitivity as a primary result rather than relegating it to a robustness check.
